content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a method to disentangle controllable and uncontrollable features for reinforcement learning tasks. The proposed method is shown to be promising in representation learning in the sense of its usage in downstream policy optimization and planning. The proposed method is composed of reconstruction and disentanglement. The resulting representation also exhibits good interpretation ability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
- The proposed method is intuitive, straightforward, and effective.
- A series of experiments are conduct to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

## Weaknesses 
1. One of the most concern I have is the similarity between this work and [1]. Both works share a similar idea, which is to improve representation for downstream control tasks through a different treatment on controllable and uncontrollable features. Regarding low-level technique details, both works use action input for controllable part prediction, while [1] uses a probabilistic modeling which generalizes the deterministic modeling of this work (if the Gaussian distribution used in [1] uses fixed variance, its KL term would be the effectively similar as the Lc and Lu in this work).
2. The entropy loss term L_H is a bit hand-waving and would thus be unstable to me. There are more principled ways of entropy estimation, such as the non-parametric methods in [2]. 
3. The experiments are mostly in a toy domain, and it is hard to tell the capability of disentanglement under more realistic scenarios such as the visual noisy environments in [1].


[1] Denoised MDPs: Learning World Models Better Than The World. Tongzhou Wang, Simon S. Du, Antonio Torralba, Phillip Isola, Amy Zhang, Yuandong Tian
[2] CALIBRATING ENERGY-BASED GENERATIVE ADVER- SARIAL NETWORKS. Zihang Dai, Amjad Almahairi, Philip Bachman, Eduard Hovy & Aaron Courville
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written in general. The novelty is limited, since similar ideas have been explored in [1] and also the TIA work (which is already cited in the submission). The implementation details are present in the submission.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem of learning controllable representation for RL is quite important. This paper propose a reasonable algorithm to address this issue, but I am not convinced of its novelty (since other previous work have already achieved more realistic application performance) and impact.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2960 by Reviewer S58A

content.title: Reviewer S58A
content.comment:
First, we would like to thank the reviewer for the time spent and the review. We would like to discuss your points of concern:

- We saw that there is 1 small mistake in the summary of the paper, as we do not employ reconstruction in our algorithm.

1) This work had not caught our attention prior to submission, as it is relatively new. You are correct that it exhibits many similarities to our work and that the algorithm looks like it has been created with a similar idea in mind; latent-space separation, with an action-conditioned prediction for controllable states, and a state-only prediction for uncontrollable states. That being said, we do think that there are fundamental differences in our work: we try to tackle the problem of separating controllable from uncontrollable features into an explicit, structured latent representation. If you look at the latent sizes in [1], they are well over 200 neurons, which means that we probably cannot infer any interpretable meaning from the neurons themselves, but need a decoder to portray the information that is being kept inside them. This means that we could not use, for example, planning with constraints on a subset of the neurons.

2) We thank the reviewer for his advice. We agree with the reviewer that our entropy loss is not a very intuitive way of avoiding collapse when dealing with forward prediction gradients, but it is helpful in pushing apart the neurons in order to get structure in the latent representation; preliminary tests using a reconstruction loss resulted in less structured representations. We think this is because a simple distance metric between samples allows for re-arrangements in latent space during training, while a decoder is less flexible as it needs its input to remain relatively constant for the same observation. Furthermore, we now see that there might be some misunderstanding when using the word entropy, as ‘contrastive’ would be a better-suited definition. We have therefore updated this throughout our paper.

3) Unlike [1] and [2], we have not focused on performance, but rather on keeping an interpretable, structured representation in MDPs by means of separating controllable from uncontrollable features. There is not a lot of related work in this direction [3][4][5][6], as this line of research still seems to be in an early stage. We have therefore not focused on more complex environments than a procedurally generated maze, but this is an interesting venue for future work.

We would kindly ask you to reconsider your score given our replies. If there are any other concerns, we would be glad to discuss them.


[1] Denoised MDPs: Learning World Models Better Than The World. Tongzhou Wang, Simon S. Du, Antonio Torralba, Phillip Isola, Amy Zhang, Yuandong Tian
[2]  Xiang Fu, Ge Yang, Pulkit Agrawal, and Tommi Jaakkola. Learning task informed abstractions
[3] Valentin Thomas, Jules Pondard, Emmanuel Bengio, Marc Sarfati, Philippe Beaudoin, Marie-Jean Meurs, Joelle Pineau, Doina Precup, and Yoshua Bengio. Independently Controllable Factors.
[4] Vincent Francois-Lavet, Yoshua Bengio, Doina Precup, and Joelle Pineau. Combined Reinforcement Learning via Abstract Representations. AAAI2019
[5] Thomas Kipf, Elise van der Pol, and Max Welling. Contrastive Learning of Structured World Models. ICLR2020
[6] Weakly Supervised Representation Learning with Sparse Perturbations. Kartik Ahuja, Jason Hartford, Yoshua Bengio. NIPS 2022

content.title: Thanks for your response

Thanks for the detailed response. 
I appreciate the authors' effort on developing interpretable and structural representation in an RL setting. However, I think the methodology is very similar to [1] and thus I think if with a smaller number of latent dimension by design, [1] will also exhibit some disentangled properties. content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors focus on the task of learning separate representations for the controllable and uncontrollable part in an RL setting. To do so, the authors follow a two-step approach: they design an action conditioned forward model to learn the controllable part (section 3.1) and a forward prediction model, given information on the controllable part, that learn the uncontrollable part (section 3.2). Further, the authors add a term to the loss function that should prevent the mode collapse that may arise. In section 4, the authors test their approach on simple and pixel-based RL tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros.
-) The authors study an interesting and relevant problem for the RL community. For safely applying RL I believe it would be necessary to develop debugging tools. A crucial one would be to develop an ability to identify what parts of the environment are controllable.
-) The two-step approach is quite intuitive in general.

Cons.
-) The algorithm has no rigorous motivation. In general, it is well known that the forward model is not a good objective for filtering uncontrollable noise (see https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08847, failure of existing approaches). I do not think the authors established any mathematical motivation for way their approach should work.
-) The two-step approach is quite intricate since the second step relies on the success of the first step. This can make the algorithm be not robust.
-) The experiments are quite basic and do not focus on a challenging problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
-) The problem and the motivation for it are well described.  
-) The mathematical reasoning for why the approach should work is very rudimentary and should be improved in my opinion. 
-) There are some missing references. Recently there were several papers that studied the problem of uncontrollable process which is a part of the input space. The authors should refer to these works and highlight the differences/ how they circumvent the counter example raised in these works (and especially here https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08847):
1) https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08847.
2) https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.15477.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe this paper poses an interesting problem. However, the lack of mathematical rigour and the fact the experiments are quite rudimentary at the current point led me to vote for a reject. Further, I believe the authors should better highlight current literature on this topic.

content.title: Reviewer 7kjZ
content.comment:
We would first like to thank the reviewer for the time spent and effort spent in making the review. We will discuss your points here:

- There is 1 small mistake in the summary of the paper, as the uncontrollable forward prediction does not rely on the controllable features z^{c}, but only on the uncontrollable features z^{u}.

1) Lack of Rigorous motivation: Forward model not filtering uncontrollable noise - We agree with the reviewer that an action-conditioned forward prediction model by itself is not sufficient to filter out all uncontrollable noise. It has not been our main research focus to create an algorithm that achieves high rewards in distracting environments, but rather disentangle an MDP into structured controllable and uncontrollable features, and show a potential use for this disentanglement: Planning in a module of the latent space.

2) Non-robust 2-step approach: Could you elaborate on which part of the algorithm you are referring to by a 2-step approach?

3) Basic Experiments / Problem: Literature on structured, interpretable representations is, to our best knowledge, quite limited [3][4][5][6]. We understand that our experiments are not done in high-dimensional, distracting environments, but to our best knowledge, we are the first to explicitly separate the encoded output of pixel observations of three MDPs into interpretable controllable and uncontrollable features. 

4) Missing references / Highlight differences: We were not aware of these works at the time of submission, but we thank you for the additions and will add [1] and [2] to our related work. As for the differences: The first is that [1] and [2] both use a decoder. Furthermore, [1] is focused on performance in distracting environments and has a latent state size of over 200 neurons, which means that there is no interpretable structure present in the neurons themselves, but a decoder is needed to estimate the latent information present. Furthermore, in contrast to [2],  we do not focus on exogenous vs endogenous features, and we are not able to investigate and compare our representation when trained with [2], as the source code is not available. We do however agree with the reviewer that, as said before, a simple forward model will not be sufficient when dealing with distracting environments. 

We hope to have clarified some of your concerns. Could our replies convince you to increase your score or do you have more concerns about the scientific contributions of our work?

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors study the problem of interpretable reinforcement learning for high-dimensional control by decomposing the underlying latent representations into "controllable" and "uncontrollable" components. The fundamental hypothesis of the work involves defining auxiliary learning objectives to pretrain encoders that provide suitable representations sufficient for downstream control tasks while also learning action-independent environment-specific features. To achieve this, the authors suggest a mixture of auxiliary losses, including 
(i) a next-state prediction loss conditioned on actions (for controllable features)
(ii) a next-state prediction loss independent of actions (for uncontrollable features)
(iii) an adversarial loss, to reduce information leak b/w "controllable," "uncontrollable" features
Using a maze environment, the authors provide some experiments to evaluate the learned representations' interpretability qualitatively.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Some strengths of the current draft include the following:
+ The problem is well-motivated and timely; learning interpretable representations for RL could improve the application in safety-critical settings.
+ The authors provide some ablations to measure the utility of their proposed losses' components.


The current draft has several avenues for improvement; some weaknesses are listed below:
- Experiments are limited and provide evidence only on maze-navigation tasks. While great for motivating the problem, it is crucial to have evidence on more high-dimensional and complex control tasks.
- Beyond ablations, including head-to-head comparisons to existing algorithms in the literature (or variants as relevant) would be very helpful in assessing the proposed methods' actual improvements over current literature.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper presents some novel ideas. However, improving the presentation and writing could significantly enhance the current draft. It is hard to disentangle the core contributions of this work from the existing literature on unsupervised representation learning for reinforcement learning. In particular, the authors are encouraged to present their ideas in the context of existing literature (including contrastive losses for RL representation learning) and highlight the limitations of current approaches. It would also be quite helpful to include comparisons to existing algorithms in the literature as baselines and evaluation on more complex environments (beyond the maze, which is great to motivate the ideas but insufficient to assess the utility of the presented approach).
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors suggest a mixture of auxiliary losses for pretraining encoders that provide interpretable features for reinforcement learning. The ideas are evaluated on a synthetic task (maze navigation), with some qualitative assessments on the interpretability of different feature heads. The authors are encouraged to improve the presentation of core ideas and include experiments on more complex environments to support the generality of the algorithm.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

We like to thank the reviewer for the time spent in making the review. We will try to discuss your points one by one.

Evidence on high-dimensional and complex control tasks - The main goal of our paper was to obtain an interpretable representation in MDPs, by separating controllable features from uncontrollable features in a single encoder. Please correct us if we are missing a certain paper, but we believe that there is currently no algorithm that is suited for an objective comparison.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2960 by Reviewer QPR4

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a method for learning lower-dimensional representation of the state with the goal of obtaining greater interpretability of representation, which separates the learned features into controllable and uncontrollable dimensions. These features are learned from rollouts of random policy using several next-state prediction losses, with the separation enforced by having only the prediction of controllable features depend on the action and removing projections of uncontrollable features with an adversarial loss. 

The experiments are performed on simple environments with pixel observations: either maze environments with different layouts or catch. The authors train an agent with DDQN and find that the proposed method results in more interpretable representations while not harming performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Two main claims of the paper are that: (a) learning a low-dimensional state representation that separates controllable and uncontrollable features results in greater interpretability, and (b) greater interpretability obtained in this manner does not trade-off with the performance.

Neither of the claims is clearly true a priori and by evaluating on only two simple environments (catch and mazes; without any noise or distractor objects), the authors do not substantiate these claims beyond these very limited settings. While the state space considered there are images, the sufficient statistics in these environments are very low dimensional and easily deduced (position of ball and pad in catch; positions of walls and agent in maze); hence the dimensionality of latent representation can be easily determined and much more easily interpreted. While it is a good sign that learned representations do seem to capture these sufficient statistics and I'm glad the authors started by experimenting on simple environments, it is currently unclear: (a) how one can determine the dimensionality of compressed features in the general case (when the sufficient statistics are unknown), (b) whether the higher-dimensional features will also be interpretable, and (c) if (for the purposes of interpretability) the dimensions of compressed features are lower than the dimensions of sufficient statistics, is the performance still going to be intact? Note also that the claim that the proposed method does not affect performance is substantiated in only one experiment (Fig 5), which is insufficient.  

Furthermore, because the dimensionality of controllable features is low in this case -- and all the controllable features happen to also be relevant for reward, what happens when there are multiple controllable features that aren't useful for obtaining the reward? This is for example the case with Mujoco Ant, and looking at the results in DIAYN (Eysenbach et al, 2018), it seems likely that by optimizing the representation for capturing easily controllable features, one is likely to miss the harder-to-capture but necessary for performance features and approach like one proposed here would end up hurting the downstream performance. Similarly, many environments contain many task-irrelevant, uncontrollable but predictable features (e.g. patterns in the background of ProcGen); and seems likely that reward-agnostic methods like the one proposed here would again fail to capture reward-relevant over easily predicted features. 

In terms of baselines, I'm glad the authors are including a comparison to inverse prediction loss, however, in order to make the paper stronger, it would be good to include a comparison to other interpretability methods and at least some other methods you cited that provide auxiliary losses that shape representation during DRL training. 

Given claims of interpretability are so central to this paper, the related work section does not provide good coverage of prior interpretability work in DRL. Papers included in this survey [1] could provide inspiration for environments to examine your method on, specifically, it would be interesting to see the results on more complex Atari environments (as in [2]) and Mujoco Ant / ProcGen (for the reasons outlined in the previous paragraph). 

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.13112
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00138
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While the specific combination of prediction and adversarial losses is novel to my knowledge, each of the individual components is not particularly novel (as noted in the Related Work). The formulation of entropy loss in equation (4) is odd (the loss penalizes the distance of latent representation to a random sample whose variance is determined by batch size), I wonder what motivated this choice and why not use a more standard entropy loss? 

The paper is relatively clear. To improve the clarity and reproducibility of the paper, I suggest the following:
- list all relevant hyperparameters in a table
- run hyper-parameter sweeps and report how sensitive the results are to the choice of hyperparameters
- in all figures, especially Fig 2, make the caption of the figure more descriptive, the figures should be understandable on their own
- in Fig 1b: explain the meaning of different colors 
- in Fig 1, 3, 4: label the axis
- a graph of the entire architecture in the appendix would be also helpful.
content.summary_of_the_review: Two main claims of the paper are that: (a) learning a low-dimensional state representation that separates controllable and uncontrollable features results in greater interpretability, and (b) greater interpretability obtained in this manner does not trade-off with the performance. Neither of the claims is clearly true a priori and by evaluating on only two simple environments (catch and mazes; without any noise or distractor objects), the authors do not substantiate these claims beyond these very limited settings.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2960 by Reviewer QPR4

content.title: Reviewer QPR4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the extensive review. We would like to discuss some of the concerns addressed by the reviewer.

(a) how one can determine the dimensionality of compressed features in the general case (when the sufficient statistics are unknown) - We believe that this is still in general an open question in representation learning. In the different examples, the encoder (including the dimension of the final layer) is selected by us as a hyper-parameter based on some prior estimations about the task at hand. We have now added this to our discussion section.

(b) whether the higher-dimensional features will also be interpretable - When training a representation with our algorithm, the neurons take up an arbitrary ordering; neuron 1 can be the x-position of the agent in 1 seed, and the y-position in another seed. A high-dimensional latent representation would therefore be harder to interpret. However, as in [1], additional interpretability losses could be added with prior knowledge, forcing some neurons to have a predefined relation to a certain action. We have also added our thoughts about this to the discussion section.

(c) if (for the purposes of interpretability) the dimensions of compressed features are lower than the dimensions of sufficient statistics, is the performance still going to be intact? - We believe that when the dimensions of compressed features are lower than the minimal dimension of sufficient statistics, we are potentially losing necessary information which can negatively affect performance. Like (a) and (b), we have added some of the pitfalls of interpretability in latent representations to our discussion. 

Related work on prior interpretability - On a more precise level, we do not see many similarities between works in [2] and our work. [2] also does not seem to show any representation or visualisations thereof, making it difficult to go through each of the 261 papers mentioned. However, we agree with the reviewer that on a high level, the survey paper should be mentioned and have added a reference to [2] in our discussion.

Reproducibility - We have added more ablations on the hyperparameters in the Appendix; learning rates, z^{u} detachment and residual prediction ablations. Also, we thank the reviewer for the observations on the figures and have made Fig.2 more descriptive and explained the colors in Fig. 1. As for labelling the axis, we don’t think labels for every figure will improve figure presentation, as most figures consist of a large set of subfigures. We do however describe the figure columns in the caption and have updated some figure explanations to explain the axes. Furthermore, as for reproducibility, we have made an anonymous Github repository at: https://github.com/iclr2023submission1/anonymous_repo.

We hope to have clarified some of your concerns. Do you think that our replies could lead to an increase in your score or do you have any remaining concerns about the scientific contribution of the paper?



[1] Vincent Francois-Lavet, Yoshua Bengio, Doina Precup, and Joelle Pineau. Combined Reinforcement Learning via Abstract Representations. AAAI2019
[2] A Survey on Interpretable Reinforcement Learning. Claire Glanois, Paul Weng, Matthieu Zimmer, Dong Li, Tianpei Yang, Jianye Hao, Wulong Liu

content.title: Response to the authors
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for a detailed response, in particular, for adding clarifications and improving the plots. 

My main concerns regarding the paper are still there (evaluation on only two simple environments) and whether the proposed method may harm the performance in the general case (see examples and arguments in my review). 

Consequently, I'm maintaining the original score for the paper.

content.title: General comment to the reviewers.
content.comment:
We would like to express our thanks to all the reviewers for their reviews, time and effort. We have updated our related work section with the papers provided and have extended the discussion section to further explain the pitfalls of interpretability in MDP representations. Also, we have added more ablations on hyperparameters in the Appendix and have added more detail to the caption of Figure 2.

We would however again like to emphasize that the main goal of our research was not to improve downstream performance over current representation learning algorithms but to progress the field of interpretable, structured representation learning in MDPs and show a use for these representations in terms of downstream algorithms like reinforcement learning. As also said in our individual responses, the literature regarding this field is quite limited, which complicates comparisons between other work in terms of visualisation and/or performance.

Lastly, we have added an anonymous GitHub repository with our code at https://github.com/iclr2023submission1/anonymous_repo.
